newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. envoy in Seoul quits, citing personal reasons.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy in Seoul quits, citing personal reasons.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to South Korea, James Laney, who steered sometimes rocky ties with Seoul while promoting Washington's opening to North Korea, said he had submitted his resignation on Tuesday.
In a written statement, Laney said he was leaving for personal reasons and had asked U.S. President Bill Clinton to accept his resignation.
"Since I took the position as Ambassador almost four years ago, it has been my plan to leave after President Clinton's first term," he said.
"In particular, I promised my family that I would be back home in early 1997. I have always intended to keep that promise."
Laney said he was leaving when the "Korean-American alliance and the cooperation between our two governments are the strongest they have ever been".
Yet during his tenure, U.S. ties with Seoul have been complicated by a policy of cautious engagement with North Korea that has left South Koreans anxious over U.S. intentions.

Laney was in the centre of a furore after former U.S. secretary of state Warren Christopher reacted to the intrusion of a North Korean submarine into Southern waters in September by urging restraint on "both sides".
On North Korea, Laney advanced U.S. policy by arguing strongly that relations with Pyongyang should reflect its growing weakness.
After years focussing on North Korea's military might, he argued that the country's decrepitude posed a new threat, which was best met by combining military deterrence with engagement.
The fruit of that policy was a landmark 1994 agreement with Pyongyang that eased North Korea's nuclear menace.
